analysis.title: How Many "Once-In-A-Lifetime" Days Can One Year Have?
key_insights: Thursday's Nasdaq 100 crash was a 4.9 standard deviation move per Goldman's Mark Wilson, roughly a once-in-8,000-years event if returns were normally distributed. The year has also produced the worst Nasdaq day since Covid, the biggest put day in Cboe history and a VVIX move topped only by Volmageddon.
Wilson says the vol of VIX had its second-largest one-day move ever, the largest number of US index puts ever traded, and the S&P had a 4 std dev move, one of the largest in decades.

Wilson's explanation: over half of stocks are passively owned, and much of daily volume comes from price-agnostic trading (quant, systematic, index and fund rebalancing, ETF/factor strategies). The fastest fundamental managers run leveraged, tightly risk-managed strategies on similar risk models. On a shrinking denominator, a similarly behaving cohort can cause moves that standard sigma distributions say are improbable.
Thursday flows: Nomura's McElligott estimated $47B of levered ETF selling and $61B of vol-control supply. Goldman's desk saw ETFs take 32% of the tape.

Diversification has weakened: Wilson flagged that Apple, the largest index stock, is now negatively correlated with the Nasdaq, and the S&P 500 has only a 60% correlation with its equal-weight version. Nvidia realized 100 vol over five days.
The SMH five-day return fell to roughly -20%, matching the March 2020 low as the worst on the chart going back to 2011.

Goldman's estimate of Thursday client performance: fundamental TMT funds lost 410bps (a -2.8 standard deviation day) and multi-strats lost 142bps (assuming 4.5x leverage and no fees). Only systematic funds made money, barely. The loss wiped out the TMT crowd's 2026 gain, which was about +24% before the June/July AI selloff.
Goldman's high-beta momentum factor has a drawdown of more than 30% over four weeks (-33.7% from the late-September peak), is down 15% YTD and more than 50% from its Q2 high.
Goldman's US broad AI basket (GSTMTAIP) had its worst day since March 2020. The unconstrained TMT momentum pair (GSTMTMOM) posted its tenth -10pp day this year.
Goldman's vol panic index hit 9.57 out of 10, in the panic zone, the biggest two-day round trip on record after Wednesday's relief rally.

Goldman Prime: de-grossing in eight of the last nine sessions and four straight sessions globally. Net selling was the largest in two weeks (-1.6 standard deviations), with long sales outpacing short sales 2.2 to 1.

Fundamental L/S net leverage (beta-adjusted) fell 7.6 points on the week to 57.2%, down 14.1 points YTD, the lowest since May 2025 (4th percentile on three years, 19th on five). Overall Prime net leverage is in the 4th percentile on one year (37th on five), per Goldman's Vincent Lin.

Bull case: the same crowd that forced the 4.9-sigma day down has to buy back once vol falls. Wilson expects the AI story to take a less prominent role after the selloff and volatility to decline as exposures shrink, and does not expect NVDA to realize 100 vol again in the next 5 days.
Goldman's Miller desk likes owning the rebound in Hyperscalers (GSXUHYPR) as stocks approach washout levels, via a GSXUHYPR Jan 110/120 call spread costing 1.8%.

Friday: chips bounced but breadth did not. The Nasdaq rose on short covering in the most-sold names while most S&P stocks finished red. Payrolls of 165K ended the growth scare but put a December rate hike back on the table.

Author view: the market structure issues (passive over half, ETFs a third of the tape, same risk models) were not fixed, so another 4.9-sigma day is possible. Positioning is clean enough for a bounce, but the 1998 analog had three Fed cuts in seven weeks, while now there is a hot payrolls print and a possible December hike. The rebound is expected to be fast, crowded and short-lived.

tension_points.bull_case: Positioning is light: net leverage at an 18-month low and nine days of de-grossing. The crowd running the same risk models must buy back as vol falls, and Goldman's desk likes the Hyperscalers rebound.
tension_points.bear_case: The shrinking-denominator market structure is unchanged (passive over half, ETFs a third of the tape). Hot payrolls put a December hike back on the table, and the rebound may be fast, crowded and short-lived.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A Fed that does not cut, unlike 1998 when it cut three times in seven weeks. A December rate hike would undermine the bounce.
